The GPS satellites orbit the Earth at a distance that’s called the “LEO” or “Largest Elliptical Loop” zone. This makes good sense from the perspective of the GPS system. It can't pinpoint a device that’s “too far away” or the signals will be confused. 
Also there’s a “Constellation” orbit that has a more direct, lower-Earth orbit. This enables direct satellite coverage of the North American continent and most of Asia. 
GPS works by “constellations”, the signals from the Global Navigation Satellite System satellites are superimposed on each other, which enables them all to have unique signals.  We usually think of GPS as being three-orphan GPS satellites (the US, France, and the UK) and then four-beacons, but even these are different constellations or “gradiometers”. For a more detailed description of this concept, there’s a short 3-minute TED talk by Martin Fisher:
http://www.ted.com/talks/martin_fisher_the_google_space_of_objects_1085873?language=en
